title: API degradation field guide (WIP)
summary: Working runbook draft for common API degradations: client timeouts, request throttling (429), degraded streaming quality/throughput, and spikes in 5xx/error rates. Intended as a pragmatic on-call checklist with quick mitigations, telemetry to check, and follow-up tasks.
scope: Applies to Redwood hosted API endpoints and edge gateways; notes include fallback patterns used by Dedicated clusters. Not intended to replace product-specific playbooks (see linked artifacts).
quick_triage_steps: Confirm alert: note alert name, start time, and the primary symptom (latency / spike in 5xx / rise in 429 / streaming stalls).
Check global status page and internal outage channel (Slack #incidents) to see if already acknowledged.
Identify blast radius: which routes/models/customers/regions are affected (use per-route dashboard).
Determine severity (P0/P1) and assign on-call responder + communications lead.
metrics_to_check: Request rate (RPS) by route and model - compare to baseline (last 24h medians).
p50/p95/p99 latency and tail latencies; 95->99 delta is critical for tail issues.
Error breakdown: 5xx types, 4xx incl 429s, streaming disconnects. Correlate with client retries.
Queue/backlog lengths and worker utilization (GPU util, proc queue length).
Autoscaler events (scale up/down), OOMs, pod restarts, and recent deploys.
run_commands: kubectl -n api get pods -o wide --selector=route=<route-name> (check restarts & node).
Check tracing: open trace for a slow /5xx request, verify KV cache misses and kernel latency spans.
immediate_mitigations: If tail latency spike: temporarily reduce max_batch_size and max_wait_ms on affected route to lower queuing latency.
If 429s across customers: enable emergency rate-limiter-relax policy for premium tiers OR enable degraded model routing (smaller model variant) for non-critical traffic.
If streaming stalls: toggle fallback to chunked delivery (disable multiplexed stream) and restart streaming workers on the affected pool.
If 5xx surge caused by a recent deploy: rollback the deploy or route traffic to previous version using canary rollback knob in Console.
If GPU OOMs or node failures: cordon node, migrate pods, and scale up capacity if autoscaler lagging. Monitor for thrashing.
detailed_play: Step A - Isolate the failure domain: use per-route filter to narrow to route/model/region/customer. If only one model variant, follow model-oncall; if multiple, suspect shared infra.
Step B - Check fallback paths: verify fallback routing rules are active (console -> routing -> fallbacks). If fallbacks misconfigured, enable manual fallback to compatible variant.
Step C - Backpressure controls: inspect edge gateway buffers and burst tokens. For sustained overload, enable circuit-breaker for low-priority routes.
Step D - Storage/KV health: confirm prefix cache hits && key-value backend latency; cache misses often explain token regen spikes during chat sessions.
Step E - Investigate long tail: correlate request size, input token counts, and client retry patterns. Large inputs may amplify batching mismatches.
streaming_specific: Symptoms: partial chunks then disconnects, long initial-first-byte, or continuous small-chunk delays.
Telemetry: monitor stream RTT, chunk sizes, and keepalive pings; check TCP retransmits and proxy timeouts.
Quick fixes: shorten idle timeout settings on gateway, enable chunked fallback, and restart streaming dispatchers for the pool.
Longer-term: add per-connection congestion controls in runtime, improve prefetching of KV cache for long chats.
429_specific: Symptoms: client receives 429s sporadically or in waves; often accompanied by queue growth metrics.
Check: map which internal rate-limiter emitted the 429 (edge vs runtime vs model quota).
Mitigations: temporarily increase quota for affected customers only after manual approval; adjust token bucket refill rates if safe.
Rate-limiter debugging: use debug endpoint /rates/debug?route=<route> to inspect token usage by key.
timeout_specific: Symptoms: upstream timeouts, hedging not triggering, or end-to-end latency beyond client TTLs.
Immediate: enable hedging for critical routes (send duplicate to faster region) and reduce client-side deadlines if too aggressive.
Investigate: trace to see which span dominates (compilation/kernel vs IO vs kv-backend).
Remedy: adjust kernel selection thresholds or route to a quantized variant with lower runtime latency for high-p50 workloads.
post_incident_actions: Acknowledge incident and add initial incident summary in #incidents with links to dashboards/traces.
Within 48 hours: run a short RCA draft (who/what/root cause/impact/duration) and assign owners for fixes.
Actions: add missing observability (per-route p99 heatmaps, per-customer 429 metrics), and create tickets for config hardening.
Runbook updates: capture which mitigations worked, update this doc with concrete knobs and exact commands used.
open_questions: Do we have per-tenant capacity isolation for shared pools? (affects 429 mitigation policy).
Can the autoscaler make decisions fast enough for short-lived traffic spikes? If not, consider burst pools.
Should we expose a safe emergency toggle for support to shift small customers to low-cost degraded models?
